population.note: FICTIONAL. Counts all incretin use (obesity, diabetes, cardiac, OSA, CKD). 22.9% of ~265M adults ≈ 60.7M current users. Arithmetic: ever 29 − current 22.9 = 6.1 pts used-and-off now; of the 29 pts ever-users ~17.4 pts (60%) have stopped at least once, so 17.4 − 6.1 = 11.3 pts stopped and are back on (11.3/29 = 39% of ever-users cycled; 11.3/17.4 = 65% cumulative multi-year restart, consistent with 36–47% restarting within one year compounded over several years); 29 − 17.4 = 11.6 pts never stopped; 11.6 + 11.3 = 22.9 current. Payer split of ~60.7M current users: ~20M on diabetes/cardiac/OSA/CKD codes across commercial, Part D and Medicaid; ~11M under employer weight-management benefits; ~2.6M Medicare obesity (Bridge successor model); ~1.9M Medicaid obesity in opted-in states; ~22M cash-pay via TrumpRx and manufacturer direct; ~3M gray (personal importation from Canada/Mexico, residual compounding). Age bands weighted by adult population (~20/33/24/23%) give ≈22.8%. Income thirds average ≈22.8%; the bottom third is propped up by diabetes coding and Medicaid, the middle third is the one most exposed to employer retreat and pays cash. Off-drug populations: ~16M adults have used and are off now (6.1%), most citing cost or GI effects; roughly 45M adults with obesity have never been on a drug, concentrated in the bottom third and in states without Medicaid obesity coverage. US adult obesity est. ~33.5% (from 36.4% in 2026), with the fall concentrated in the top income third. Pediatric: ~800k under-18s on drug (≈1.1% of ~73M), ~85% of them aged 12–17; under-12 use is now on-label (liraglutide 6–11 from 2027) but still about 0.15% of children 6–11, and still skews to upper-income and Medicaid-EPSDT families with specialist access.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot ran to Dec 2027 and was replaced on Jan 1, 2028 by a CMMI obesity model at the same ~$245/month Medicare payment and ~$50 copay, now with continuation rules (≥5% loss at 6 months or ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered). ~2.6M beneficiaries use it: 2.6M × $245 × 12 ≈ $7.6B/year Medicare spend, running ahead of the CBO 2026–2034 '≥$35B' pace (~$4B/yr). Medicaid: 23 states cover obesity GLP-1s at the $245 rate; ~1.9M enrollees × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.6B/year total, ~$3.9B federal at a ~70% blended match. Seven of those states run Section 1115 waivers that condition coverage on monitored adherence. Diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA and CKD indications remain covered under ordinary Part D and Medicaid rules.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 60+ generic semaglutide brands at ~$6–40/month. Canada: five generic semaglutide makers, ~CAD 60–95/month. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and much of Southeast Asia have generics; cost-plus injectable semaglutide is available in ~170 countries. Generic oral semaglutide is launching in India in 2028. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: Managed decline: TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct cash prices are now $149 (oral starting doses, Foundayo and Wegovy pill) to $299 (top-dose injectables). Wegovy cash is $199–249, Zepbound vials $249–299. Retatrutide launched in 2028 at $499–649/month cash, which is the high end of the range. List prices ($1,349 Wegovy) still exist only for PBM rebate math. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 44% (Business Group on Health 2028). Most remaining plans cover only with BMI≥35 or a comorbidity code, plus enrolment in a monitored lifestyle vendor. 2027–28 claim audits found coding drift toward 'prediabetes' and 'OSA' to get coverage. The 503B exclusion of semaglutide and tirzepatide was finalised in Jan 2027, so compounding is mostly gone. Personal importation of Canadian generics by mail sits in an FDA enforcement grey zone (~3M users). By volume, weekly pens make up ~55% of fills and daily orals ~45%. Orals dominate the cash channel.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, Lilly; approved Mar 2028)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, Novo; approved Jan 2027, modest uptake)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics; now labelled for ages 6+)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (liraglutide, Jun 2027; semaglutide, Sep 2028)
alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed, not FDA-labelled (ASAM and VA/DoD guidance, Oct 2027, semaglutide as an option for AUD with comorbid obesity or T2D; Novo sNDA for AUD filed Jun 2028)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol use disorder without obesity, prescribed by addiction clinics citing the 2027 guidelines
microdosing / 'metabolic maintenance' low-dose orals bought cash via telehealth by people without obesity
nicotine and gambling craving reduction, observational and anecdotal
maintenance low-dose oral after injectable loss, to dampen regain
drugs.pipeline_note: CagriSema (under review at start) was approved Jan 2027 but trails tirzepatide and sells mainly where Novo offers rebates. Retatrutide (phase 3 at start) had its BLA filed Feb 2027 and was approved Mar 2028, 13 months after filing. It is labelled at ~28% mean loss at 80 weeks, up to ~30% in BMI≥35, with dysesthesia and an uncommon apathy/anhedonia line in adverse reactions, and is cash-priced $499–649. This is how the 'triple_agonist_30pct' driver is realised: surgical-grade loss from a pen for people who can pay. Survodutide was filed Sep 2027, decision expected 2029 at the earliest. Amycretin is in phase 3, no filing, not on the US market. MariTide monthly injectable and the bimagrumab muscle-preserving adjuncts are still in trials and not marketed. The GLP-1R field is still crowded with competitors, but the US market remains a Lilly–Novo duopoly. Global incretin revenue ~$118B in 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Retatrutide's higher doses raised GI discontinuation, and slower titration schedules are now standard.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; more visible with ~28% loss on retatrutide.
Still no causal confirmation in long-term RCTs; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; multidistrict litigation continues, no class verdict.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–40% of lost weight is lean mass depending on age and protein/resistance training. 2027–28 cohort data link it to falls and fractures in users 70+. The effect is socially visible as 'soft-thin' in users without training access.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA added a label recommendation (2027) for baseline assessment and resistance exercise counselling in older adults. No approved adjunct.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Pooled 2026–27 cohort and pharmacovigilance analyses converged on roughly a doubling of relative risk. Absolute risk is still low, on the order of a few extra cases per 10,000 patient-years, higher in people with diabetes and small optic discs. Ophthalmology referrals rose.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class-wide Warnings and Precautions for all GLP-1 RA and incretin products (Mar 2027), up from 'very rare'. The label advises baseline eye history and prompt evaluation of sudden vision loss. EMA aligned in 2027. A vision-loss litigation wave has been filed.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal in larger 2027 datasets.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Retatrutide phase 3 safety tables recorded apathy/anhedonia as 'uncommon' (~1% vs ~0.4% placebo). Clinic surveys suggest a few percent of users describe it; dose reduction often relieves it. Prevalence across the class is still not measured.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed as an uncommon adverse reaction on the retatrutide label and the EU semaglutide SmPC. No class warning. Some obesity clinics add a one-line mood/interest screening question.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Larger real-world datasets show regain is partial and slower than STEP-1 implied, about half to two-thirds over 1–2 years. Faster regain is seen after retatrutide-scale loss.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Justifies payer continuation rules and chronic-therapy framing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D and protein insufficiency flagged in registries, concentrated in low-income users without dietitian access.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None formal; professional society nutrition guidance (2027).

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. Children aged 6–11 are now on-label with no adult-horizon data. 39% of ever-users have cycled.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric approvals carry 10-year growth, puberty and bone-density postmarketing registries.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Compounded reports have declined since the 503B exclusion. Counterfeit pens and mislabelled imported vials are now the main source.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised (Jan 2027); CBP seizures; import alerts.

safety_ledger.effect: Dysesthesia (abnormal skin sensation) with triple agonist
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Reported in a minority of retatrutide trial participants, dose-related, mostly mild and transient.

food_and_beverage.state: About a third of US households now contain a user. Volumes in salty snacks, confectionery and full-sugar soda fell ~3–4% a year in 2027–28; packaged-food makers sold or shrank indulgent brands and rebuilt around protein, fibre and 120-calorie formats. Dollar sales held better than volume thanks to price and pack-size engineering. Discount grocers serving bottom-third households saw the smallest volume change, so the income gradient now shows up in category mix.

alcohol.state: US spirits depletions fell ~4% in 2027 and beer volumes ~3%, steeper than secular trend. The 2027 addiction-medicine guidelines put a prescription in the path of the heaviest drinkers, who carry the industry's sales. Brands are pivoting to low/no-alcohol, ready-to-drink 'occasion' cans and premium small pours. Bars in affluent districts report fewer second rounds.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat to slightly down and checks smaller. Fine dining and fast-casual adopted 'small plate' and protein-forward menus and charge for experience. Value chains and buffet formats in lower-income regions lost little traffic, and some took share as menus diverged by neighbourhood income.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking: store closures at Torrid and DXL, and plus ranges cut back at department stores. Mainstream brands profit from size churn and from regain-driven re-buying. A premium 'fitted performance' tier aimed at visibly muscled bodies is growing fastest.

fitness.state: Strength training is the growth category. Boutique 'muscle-preservation' studios and coaching memberships ($150–300/month) cluster in top-third zip codes, and low-cost chains have added weight floors. Employer wellness vendors bundle connected scales and resistance programmes with GLP-1 eligibility.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 44%. Coverage is concentrating on diabetes, cardiac, OSA and CKD codes. PBMs sell 'metabolic carve-out' products with adherence monitoring. Pharmacy trend has moderated to ~8% as unit prices fall. Outcomes-based wellness surcharges tied to BMI or programme adherence are spreading among large employers.

pharma.state: Lilly is the clear volume and efficacy leader with Foundayo and retatrutide. Novo competes on price, CagriSema and the AUD filing. US net prices are falling ~15–20% a year through government channels while volume roughly doubles. Ex-US revenue is eroded by generics. Indian and Canadian generic makers are building US-ready capacity for 2031.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A thin body is read by default as treated. A thin, muscled body is read as treated and resourced, meaning cash for retatrutide or a covered injectable plus a coach. A thin, soft body reads as cheap oral or Medicaid. A large body is increasingly read as uninsured, off-drug or cycling. Eye-catching weight swings are an open marker of who lost coverage.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The top income third uses the most (28.5%) and gets the best regimen. In Charlotte, NC, banking and health-system employers kept coverage and added strength-coaching stipends, and their staff now share a visible uniform: lean, muscled, protein shaker on the desk. Retail and logistics workers in the same metro lost coverage in 2027 and pay $149–199 for orals, or stop. Torrid and DXL closures in suburban malls mark where the lost customers were. Children of the affluent are on-label at 6+ with dietitian support, and the obesity gradient between top and bottom thirds widened.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals have shrunk rather than vanished. Hosts in user-heavy circles plan 'grazing' tables and protein courses, and 'food noise' has become ordinary vocabulary. Holiday meals are now a known site of friction between on-drug and off-drug relatives. School lunch debates now include children on medication.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles in big cities list 'on Zep' or 'off-cycle' the way they once listed drinking habits. Couples where one partner loses coverage report strain over sudden regain. Some users describe muted desire; clinics treat this as uncommon and dose-related.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dial. Lacking a prescription is widely read as a choice or a failure of benefits, not of will. Drinking heavily without trying the drug is starting to be read the same way in professional settings.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Acknowledged but uncommon. Retatrutide's label lists apathy/anhedonia at ~1%. Clinicians estimate a few percent of class users notice flattening, mostly at high doses, and many recover with dose reduction. No population-scale measurement exists.
interior_life.framing: Labels and clinics call it an uncommon side effect. Addiction medicine calls the same circuitry the treatment: 'quieting the reward' is the stated rationale of the 2027 AUD guidance. The public mostly experiences it as a dosing question, not a character question.
interior_life.effect_on_work: No measurable aggregate effect. Some users in sales and hospitality describe less drive at high doses and step down. Others, including AUD patients, report steadier attendance. Employers care about adherence data for premiums, not mood.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Stand-up and online comedy run a steady seam of 'I feel nothing at brunch' jokes. A handful of musicians publicly describe tapering before recording. Bar culture in affluent districts has shifted toward 'one drink' socials, and sour, spicy and high-intensity flavours remain a user trend.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Uncommon reports of lower desire are now asked about in obesity clinics. Most couples-therapy references concern body change and coverage loss rather than flattening.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Reward blunting has no organised politics. The politics run through access and conditioning: Medicaid adherence monitoring and the US–Canada price gap. A few columnists argue a numbed electorate is easier to govern; it remains a fringe argument.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals: retatrutide, pediatric 6–11 and CagriSema all cleared. Pro-safety-labelling (the NAION class warning). Hard on compounders (503B exclusion final) while tolerating small-scale personal importation.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate to take the drug. Public subsidy at the $245/$50 rate through the Medicare CMMI obesity model and Medicaid in 23 states. TrumpRx cash channel at $149–299.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Benefits conditioning is now routine. Medicare's 2028 model continues coverage only with ≥5% loss at 6 months or ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered, verified from claims. Seven states' Medicaid 1115 waivers require ≥80% refill adherence plus a monthly cellular-scale weigh-in, and non-adherent enrollees lose obesity coverage for 12 months. ~18% of large employers run ACA outcomes-based wellness programmes that add premium surcharges (typically $40–80/month) for BMI above threshold unless the employee is enrolled in a monitored metabolic programme with connected-scale data. Privacy advocates have filed suits over scale-data sharing with vendors.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army and Air Force allow GLP-1 prescribing through military treatment facilities for members failing body-composition standards. Recruits with prior use must be off-drug and weight-stable for 90 days before accession. No civilian employment mandate. A few employers' fitness-for-duty rules now ask about vision symptoms after the NAION warning.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US–Canada price gap (US cash $199–299 vs CAD 60–95 for generics) is a campaign talking point in 2028. Lilly and Novo trade further Medicare and cash price cuts for tariff relief and approval speed. Indian manufacturers are lining up FDA-inspected capacity for the 2031–32 patent cliff.

events.event: FDA adds a class-wide NAION warning to all GLP-1 and incretin labels after pooled cohort data show roughly doubled relative risk; ophthalmologists report a rise in urgent referrals and the first vision-loss suits are filed
FDA approves liraglutide (Saxenda and generics) for obesity in children aged 6–11, with 10-year growth and puberty registries; semaglutide's 6–11 approval follows in Sep 2028

ASAM and VA/DoD guidance endorse semaglutide as an option for alcohol use disorder with comorbid obesity or type 2 diabetes; addiction clinics begin prescribing it, and spirits makers cite the guidance in profit warnings

Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge expires and is replaced by a CMMI obesity model at $245/$50 that requires claims-verified adherence or ≥5% loss for continuation; seven state Medicaid waivers add monthly cellular-scale weigh-ins
FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide, labelled at ~28% mean weight loss and up to ~30% in BMI≥35, with apathy/anhedonia listed as uncommon; cash launch $499–649/month
Gallup and KFF put current incretin use at ~23% of US adults; Business Group on Health reports employer weight-management coverage down to 44%, with remaining plans requiring comorbidity codes

open_tensions: A two-tier body economy: retatrutide plus coaching for the cash-rich, cheap orals or adherence-monitored Medicaid for the poor, and nothing for ~45M adults with obesity who are off-drug. The 2031–32 patent cliff is the only scheduled equaliser.

Benefits conditioning has turned weigh-ins and refill data into eligibility data. Privacy suits over connected scales are pending, and nobody has decided whether cycling off should cost someone a year of coverage.
Children aged 6–11 are now on-label with no adult-horizon data, while 39% of adult ever-users cycle on and off with unknown decade-scale effects.

The same reward circuitry is an uncommon labelled side effect and an endorsed alcohol treatment. A formal AUD indication would put the drug in front of heavy drinkers without obesity and test the 'niche' framing.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; brand exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
Medicare pays ~$245/month for obesity GLP-1s with a ~$50 beneficiary copay; the rate carried over unchanged from the Bridge pilot into its successor model.
Foundayo (orforglipron) and the oral Wegovy 25 mg pill are on the market, with starting doses still priced at $149 through TrumpRx and manufacturer-direct channels.
Indian generic semaglutide is still sold at roughly $8–48/month or less, and the US–India price gap is still a visible political fact.
Suicidal ideation remains debunked, and the FDA's January 2026 removal of that warning from Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound labels stands.

prose.headline: Thin Is a Salary Now: Pens, Pills and Weigh-Ins in America's Two-Tier Appetite Economy
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 nearly one American adult in four is on an incretin drug, about sixty million people, double the share of two years ago. The growth did not come from generosity. Employers kept walking away from weight-loss coverage. Fewer than half of them still cover it, and those that do want a comorbidity code and a connected scale. The doubling came from price. Through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' own storefronts, a month of oral semaglutide or Foundayo costs $149, and a top-dose Zepbound vial costs $299. List prices still exist, but only rebate spreadsheets use them. Roughly a third of users simply pay, the way they pay for a phone plan.

The drugs have stratified along with the payers. In March, Lilly's retatrutide arrived with a label promising about 28 percent weight loss, close to surgical results from a weekly pen. It costs $499 to $649 a month in cash, and few plans will touch it. In Charlotte's banking towers the new uniform is visible across a lobby: lean and deliberately muscled, a protein shaker beside the keyboard, a strength coach paid partly by the employer's wellness stipend. Six miles away, warehouse and retail workers whose coverage ended in 2027 are on cheap pills, or cycling off when money runs short, or never started. Mall landlords know where the plus-size customers went. Torrid and DXL leases are going dark in the same suburbs where discount grocers report the smallest drop in snack volume. Bodies have become legible as pay stubs, and people read them that way without saying so.

Public money carries the bottom of the market, and it now asks for proof. Medicare's pilot gave way in January to a permanent-looking model at the same $245 a month, but continuation now depends on refill data or five percent weight loss. Seven state Medicaid programmes go further, with a cellular scale in the kitchen and a weigh-in each month. Miss your refills and you lose obesity coverage for a year. About eighteen percent of large employers add a premium surcharge for a high BMI unless you join a monitored programme. Privacy lawyers are suing over who sees the scale data. The scales keep shipping.

The safety picture has hardened in one place and stayed blurry in others. The optic-nerve risk once called very rare is now a class-wide warning. The absolute risk is small, but ophthalmologists see more frightened patients, and plaintiffs' firms advertise on daytime television. Muscle loss in the elderly has its own label line. The flattening that newspapers called Ozempic personality in 2026 is now a single row in retatrutide's adverse-reaction table, uncommon at about one percent, and clinicians manage it with a lower dose. The same quieting of reward is now standard in addiction medicine. Since October 2027 the profession's guidelines have endorsed semaglutide for heavy drinkers with obesity or diabetes, and spirits companies, whose best customers are those drinkers, have revised their forecasts down a second time.

Children are part of it now. Liraglutide has been on-label for six-year-olds since mid-2027 and semaglutide since September. Use is still rare, under one in five hundred children aged six to eleven, and concentrated among families with specialists nearby. Each approval came with a ten-year registry, because nobody knows what forty years on these drugs looks like.

From the outside, much of this looks like success. Obesity is falling, pharmacy trend is cooling, and restaurants have adapted to smaller plates at higher prices. What has changed is who gets which body, and what you have to show the state or your employer to keep it. Nobody voted on that. It arrived through benefits renewals and survey data. The American price for a month of semaglutide is still several times the Canadian generic, and everyone is waiting for 2031.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renée Okafor, forty-four, steps on the gray scale before coffee because it uploads at 6 a.m. and the Ohio waiver counts the first reading. 231.4. The little light turns green. She's down eighteen pounds since the pen started in February.

In the bathroom drawer, next to her own pens, is a box of generic liraglutide for Malik, nine. He hates the daily needle less than he hates being called names at recess, and he says so. She does the injection in his thigh while he eats dry cereal, because he isn't hungry for milk anymore.

Her first client is Mr. Danko, eighty-one, on Medicare. He lost thirty pounds and now can't get out of a chair. The therapist left a sheet of sit-to-stand exercises. Renée counts him through ten. He asks if his eyes will go, because the TV keeps saying so. She says to call if anything goes dark suddenly, which is what the pharmacist told her.

At lunch she skips the drive-through without deciding to.

Her sister texts a picture from Columbus: her sister's husband at the bank's family day, arms like a man in a catalog. *Retatrutide plus a coach,* her sister writes. *Work pays half.* Renée types a thumbs-up and deletes it, then sends it anyway.

The refill reminder pings at four. Day twenty-six of twenty-eight. She drives to the CVS on Salem Avenue before shift change, because 80 percent is a number she carries now, like her PIN.

That night Malik eats half his chicken and asks if he'll be thin like Uncle Dre. She says maybe. She says eat your vegetables.
